strengths: The paper addresses a highly important and practical bottleneck in amortized neural causal discovery, which is its limited scalability to large graphs due to the high space and time complexity of attention mechanisms.

The proposed architecture, CauScale, introduces a logical and well-integrated set of modifications: a sample-dimension reduction unit, tied axial-attention weights to reduce memory, and a dual-stream (data and graph) processing block that maintains structural representation.

The empirical results are very strong, showing massive speedups (4x to 13,000x) and significant memory reduction while maintaining or improving causal discovery accuracy (e.g., achieving 96.6% mAP on 1000-node graphs).
Comprehensive evaluation and thorough ablation studies that systematically validate each design choice (e.g., the reduction unit, graph stream, graph prior, prediction head, and pooling strategy).
weaknesses: The individual architectural components are mostly adopted from existing works, such as tied attention weights from MSA Transformer (Rao et al., 2021) and the decomposed prediction head from Lippe et al. (2021). The novelty lies more in their clever integration for causal discovery than in the individual components themselves.
The training cost is quite high, requiring up to 44 hours on 8 top-tier H200 GPUs. This training footprint is substantial and should be explicitly discussed as a limitation.

The notation in Section 4.1 regarding the statistical graph prior $\rho$ is slightly confusing. If $D \in \mathbb{R}^{m \times n}$ represents the data matrix of $m$ samples and $n$ variables, the expression $(\mathbb{E}[(D - \mu)(D - \mu)^\top])^{-1}$ would yield an $m \times m$ matrix rather than the desired $n \times n$ matrix. The transpose should be applied to the first term, or $D$ should be defined as a random vector.

strengths: Strong Empirical Performance and Scalability: CauScale demonstrates impressive scaling capability, achieving fast inference on graphs with up to 1000 nodes (under 1 second) and superior mAP and AUC scores compared to state-of-the-art amortized and non-amortized baselines on both synthetic and SERGIO-GRN datasets.

Effective Memory/Time Efficiency: The incorporation of tied attention weights and a progressive reduction unit effectively mitigates the memory and computational bottlenecks of Transformer-based amortized causal discovery methods like AVICI.

Comprehensive Ablation Studies: The paper provides thorough ablation experiments evaluating the importance of different components, such as the reduction unit, graph stream, tied attention weights, and various pooling strategies.
weaknesses: Permutation Sensitivity (Lack of Sample Order Invariance): In Section 4.3, the reduction unit reshapes the data embedding along the sample dimension into chunks of size $r$ and average-pools within each chunk. Under the standard i.i.d. assumption, the order of samples carries no statistical information. However, this chunking and pooling scheme is highly sensitive to the order of samples in the input matrix. If the input samples are shuffled, the average-pooled chunks will contain different combinations of samples, leading to different representations and potentially different predicted graphs. The lack of sample permutation invariance is a significant conceptual limitation for an i.i.d. causal discovery model.

Unequal Baseline Comparison: Because AVICI encountered out-of-memory errors during training on the authors' training set, the authors evaluated AVICI using its public pre-trained checkpoints (e.g., scm-v0). This makes the comparison somewhat unfair, as AVICI was not fine-tuned or trained on the exact same distribution as CauScale.

Justification of the Inverse Covariance Prior: The statistical prior is defined as the inverse covariance (precision) matrix. While the precision matrix relates to the moral graph in Gaussian linear models, its utility degrades significantly in highly non-linear settings (e.g., the NN and Sigmoid mechanisms). The authors should discuss or evaluate how this linear prior behaves under highly non-linear causal mechanisms.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly important and practical bottleneck in causal discovery: scaling amortized/zero-shot neural causal discovery to large graphs (up to 1,000 nodes), where prior methods suffer from severe memory and runtime bottlenecks.

The proposed architecture is well-designed. The two-stream network (data stream and graph stream) cleverly incorporates data reduction along the sample dimension after a few processing layers, and leverages tied attention weights to dramatically lower the memory footprint without sacrificing representation quality.

The empirical evaluation is highly thorough, comparing against a wide range of baselines (constraint-based, score-based, FCM-based, and amortized methods) on both synthetic SCMs and realistic semi-synthetic gene regulatory network datasets (SERGIO-GRN).

The results are exceptionally strong: CauScale achieves near-perfect accuracy on in-distribution data, exhibits robust out-of-distribution generalization, and delivers enormous speedups (up to 13,000x compared to continuous optimization methods and significantly faster than prior amortized architectures).
The ablation studies are comprehensive, detailing the efficacy of the reduction unit, the two-stream structure, pooling strategies, attention mechanisms, and prediction heads.
weaknesses: The model utilizes binary intervention indicators as part of the input. It is not fully clear how the model behaves or is evaluated in purely observational settings (i.e., when no interventions are present). Clarifying this scenario would strengthen the paper.

Since the model does not explicitly enforce DAG (acyclicity) constraints during inference, the decoded graphs can contain cycles. While the authors state that real-world networks may have cycles, it would be beneficial to report the percentage of predicted graphs that violate acyclicity under the synthetic DAG settings.

The baseline AVICI is evaluated using the official pre-trained checkpoint. It is unclear if some of the performance gap is due to a distribution mismatch between AVICI's pre-training data and the test sets used here, or if it is purely an architectural advantage of CauScale. A brief discussion on this would add clarity.

strengths: Addresses a major bottleneck in amortized causal discovery (memory and time complexity) by successfully scaling neural causal discovery to large graphs with up to 1000 nodes.

Well-motivated architecture design combining hierarchical data compression (reduction unit) along the sample dimension with tied attention weights to significantly reduce both time and memory complexity.
The two-stream design (data and graph streams) combined with the data2graph block successfully mitigates representation loss during embedding compression.

Comprehensive empirical evaluation on both synthetic and realistic biological (SERGIO-GRN) datasets using a wide range of metrics, showing massive speedups (up to 13,000x over optimization-based methods) and robust out-of-distribution generalization.
Thorough ablation studies and robustness analyses (handling latent confounders, sensitivity to graph priors, and sample size analyses) that validate each major component of the proposed framework.
weaknesses: Incremental novelty of the core building blocks: several components, such as tied attention weights (Rao et al., 2021) and the pairwise prediction head (Wu et al., 2025), are adopted from existing literature.
The method remains heavily reliant on synthetic training data generated from simulated SCMs, which may limit generalization to complex real-world data-generating processes.
No explicit constraint to guarantee DAG acyclicity during prediction, relying instead on a heuristic post-hoc cycle-breaking strategy on larger graph sizes.

Sensitivity to graph prior quality: as shown in Table 4, the model's performance on large graphs (n = 1000) degrades significantly when the statistical prior is computed from a small number of samples.

strengths: Addresses a critical bottleneck in amortized causal discovery by scaling inference up to 1,000 nodes with massive speedups (up to 13,000x compared to continuous optimization baselines).

Sensible and novel architectural components, such as the progressive pooling along the sample dimension (reduction unit) which reduces redundant computation while preserving variable-wise embeddings, and the use of tied attention weights to mitigate memory overhead.
Extensive and rigorous empirical evaluation spanning synthetic datasets with various OOD settings (unseen graph sizes, noise types, and mechanisms) and semi-synthetic biological data (SERGIO-GRN).
Thorough efficiency and complexity analyses, alongside extensive ablation studies testing pooling strategies, attention types, and robustness to latent confounders and noisy priors.
weaknesses: Extremely high training cost (e.g., 37 hours on 8x NVIDIA H200 GPUs for synthetic data, and 44 hours for SERGIO-GRN), which is a common limitation of amortized models but should be explicitly highlighted and discussed.
Lack of evaluation on real-world biological datasets (e.g., the Sachs protein-signaling dataset), which are standard in the causal discovery literature.
Limited discussion on the choice of the inverse covariance matrix as the statistical graph prior in highly non-linear or non-Gaussian settings, where its reliability typically degrades.

strengths: The paper achieves significant inference speedups (up to 13,000× over non-amortized methods like NOTEARS) and demonstrates the capability to perform zero-shot causal discovery on large graphs (up to 1,000 nodes).

The empirical results on synthetic linear/non-linear datasets and semi-synthetic biological datasets (SERGIO-GRN) show strong performance in terms of mAP and SHD compared to existing amortized methods like AVICI.

The authors provide a detailed and rigorous complexity analysis (FLOP-level and peak activation memory analysis) in Section 4.6 and Appendix E, which helps clarify the theoretical efficiency of the model.
The evaluation is quite thorough, encompassing out-of-distribution (OOD) graph structures/mechanisms, robustness to latent confounders, and robustness to noisy graph priors.
weaknesses: Missing baseline for the reduction unit: The core mechanism for time efficiency is the reduction unit, which average-pools intermediate embeddings along the sample dimension. However, the authors do not compare this against a simple input-level subsampling baseline (i.e., randomly selecting m/r samples at the input stage and running the network without intermediate reduction). Without this comparison, it remains unclear whether the hierarchical reduction unit is statistically superior to basic data downsampling.

Singularity issues with the statistical graph prior: For the synthetic large-scale setting in Table 1 ($n = 1000$ and sample size $m = 1000$), the empirical covariance matrix is singular (rank at most 999). Since the model relies on the inverse covariance matrix as the statistical graph prior $\rho$, it is mathematically undefined without regularization or pseudo-inverses. The paper does not clarify how this was computed under $m \le n$ conditions, presenting a significant reproducibility and clarity issue.

Incremental architectural novelty: The technical components of CauScale are heavily derived from prior work. The tied attention mechanism is directly adopted from Rao et al. (2021), and the pairwise prediction head is taken from SEA (Wu et al., 2025). The remaining contributions (average pooling over sample chunks and a basic two-stream message passing setup) represent a relatively straightforward combination of existing ideas.

Potentially unfair comparison with AVICI at scale: The extremely low performance of AVICI on 1,000-node graphs (e.g., 0.2% mAP) is likely because the public checkpoint (`scm-v0`) was trained only on graphs up to 100 nodes. Since AVICI could not be retrained on larger scales due to out-of-memory issues, evaluating it zero-shot on $n=1000$ acts as a strawman comparison rather than a representative baseline.
